arXiv:1205.2710v1 [math.AP] 11 May 2012

Dispersion vs. anti-diffusion: well-posedness in variable coefficient and quasilinear equations of KdV-type.

David M. Ambrose Address: Department of Mathematics, Drexel University, 3141 Chestnut St., Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA Email address: ambrose@math.drexel.edu and J. Douglas Wright Address: Department of Mathematics, Drexel University, 3141 Chestnut St., Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA Email address: jdoug@math.drexel.edu
Abstract.

We study the well-posedness of the initial value problem on periodic intervals for linear and quasilinear evolution equations for which the leading-order terms have three spatial derivatives. In such equations, there is a competition between the dispersive effects which stem from the leading-order term, and anti-diffusion which stems from the lower-order terms with two spatial derivatives. We show that the dispersive effects can dominate the backwards diffusion: we find a condition which guarantees well-posedness of the initial value problem for linear, variable coefficient equations of this kind, even when such anti-diffusion is present. In fact, we show that even in the presence of localized backwards diffusion, the dispersion will in some cases lead to an overall effect of parabolic smoothing. By contrast, we also show that when our condition is violated, the backwards diffusion can dominate the dispersive effects, leading to an ill-posed initial value problem. We use these results on linear evolution equations as a guide when proving well-posedness of the initial value problem for some quasilinear equations which also exhibit this competition between dispersion and anti-diffusion: a Rosenau-Hyman compacton equation, the Harry Dym equation, and equations which arise in the numerical analysis of finite difference schemes for dispersive equations. For these quasilinear equations, the well-posedness theorem requires that the initial data be uniformly bounded away from zero.

1. Introduction

We study a family of evolution equations,

ut=a​ux​x​x+b​ux​x+ϕ,u_{t}=au_{xxx}+bu_{xx}+\phi,

where aa and bb are functions and ϕ\phi represents a collection of lower-order terms, and where x∈X=[0,M]x\in X=[0,M] and we assume uu satisfies periodic boundary conditions. We establish conditions on the coefficient functions aa and b,b, as well as conditions on ϕ,\phi, which ensure that the initial value problem for this equation is well-posed in Sobolev spaces. This is a delicate question because if there exist any xx and tt for which b<0,b<0, then formally, this term acts (locally, at least) as an anti-diffusion or backwards heat operator. The conditions we find on aa and bb indicate to what extent the dispersive effects of the leading-order term can compensate for the presence of this anti-diffusion. In a special case (in which the coefficient functions depend only on xx), we also show that if our condition is violated, then the initial value problem is ill-posed. We treat this problem for linear equations, for which aa and bb are functions of xx and t,t, and also certain quasilinear equations, for which aa and bb depend on uu and ux.u_{x}.

Our original motivation for this work is to study the question of well-posedness or ill-posedness for the the Rosenau-Hyman K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) equation,

(1) ut=2​u​ux​x​x+6​ux​ux​x+2​u​ux.u_{t}=2uu_{xxx}+6u_{x}u_{xx}+2uu_{x}.

K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) is a degenerate version of the Korteweg-de Vries equation and famously supports compactly supported traveling waves, dubbed compactons [15], as well as other non-analytic traveling waves [13]. Many papers in the literature make numerical simulations of solutions of the K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) initial value problem, focusing primarily on the study of interactions of these compactons [4], [8], [12], [16], [17]. While the existence theory for this equation remains unsettled, there is strong evidence that K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) is ill-posed for data which crosses zero [2]. Here we study a complementary problem: Is the equation well-posed when the initial condition is bounded away from zero? The answer, as we show below, is yes.

In order to show that K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) is well-posed, we first study an associated linear problem:

(2) ut=a⁡(x,t)​ux​x​x+b⁡(x,t)​ux​x+c⁡(x,t)​ux+d⁡(x,t)​u+e⁡(x,t)u_{t}=a(x,t)u_{xxx}+b(x,t)u_{xx}+c(x,t)u_{x}+d(x,t)u+e(x,t)

where once again x∈X=[0,M]x\in X=[0,M] and uu (and the coefficient functions) satisfy periodic boundary conditions. We assume that the coefficient functions are defined for all t∈[0,T],t\in[0,T], where T>0T>0.

By way of analogy, supposing that u⁡(x,0)u(x,0) is bounded away from zero in K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) we should study the situation where a⁡(x,t)a(x,t) is likewise bounded from zero. On the other hand, ux​(x,0)u_{x}(x,0) will change signs for any non-trivial periodic initial data and so we should not impose strong conditions on b⁡(x,t)b(x,t). In particular we must allow b⁡(x,t)b(x,t) to be negative, at least for some xx.

Equations like (2), and quasilinear variants, have been studied previously, though the focus has been on the case where X=𝐑X={\bf{R}} instead of the periodic problem we study here. The earliest work [6] requires that b≥0;b\geq 0; that is to say, there is no destabilizing “backwards diffusion” effect from the term b⁡(x,t)​ux​xb(x,t)u_{xx}. It is well-known that if a⁡(x,t)a(x,t) is identically zero and there is an interval on which b<0b<0, then these destabilizing effect are so pathological that (2) is ill-posed for data in Sobolev spaces. In some sense, the results of this paper are an investigation into the extent to which dispersive effects from a⁡(x,t)​ux​x​xa(x,t)u_{xxx} ameliorate the catastrophically destabilizing effects caused by a backwards diffusive term.

This question was answered for X=𝐑X={\bf{R}} in [1], and, in short, the answer is that if b⁡(⋅,t)∈L1b(\cdot,t)\in L^{1} uniformly in tt and a⁡(x,t)a(x,t) is bounded away from zero, then the dispersive effects completely dominate the backwards diffusion and the equation (including quasilinear versions) is well-posed. The issues for the periodic setting are necessarily different; the argument cannot be based on integrability (the integrability would be considered over the real line rather than a periodic interval, and a nontrivial periodic function is not integrable on the real line). The answers that we find for the periodic case include a well-posedness theorem, a parabolic smoothing result, and an ill-posedness theorem for (2), when certain conditions (primarily on aa and bb) are satisfied.

While we were motivated by the well-posedness question for the K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) equation, our method of proof applies to other quasilinear evolution equations as well. We do not attempt to give the most general theorem that we can on well-posedness of quasilinear evolution equations with nonlinear dispersion and anti-diffusion, but instead we consider some additional equations which have appeared in the literature. One of these is the Harry Dym equation, ut=u3​ux​x​x.u_{t}=u^{3}u_{xxx}. Other examples come from the numerical analysis of finite difference schemes for certain dispersive partial differential equations. We are able to prove well-posedness theorems for such equations for uniformly positive Sobolev initial data.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we study the linear problem (2) and provide sufficient conditions on the coefficients so that the equation is well-posed. The main tools here are a change of dependent variables followed by energy estimates. See Theorem 1 below for the precise statement of this result. In Section 3 we use the linear energy estimates as a inspiration for developing analogous estimates for K⁡(2,2)K(2,2). These estimates are sufficient for proving that K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) is well-posed. See Corollary 19 below for the precise statement of this result. In Section 4, we briefly discuss additional quasilinear equations which can be shown to be well-posed for positive initial data in Sobolev spaces. We mention that all of our well-posedness proofs largely follow the lines of Chapter 3 of [14], in which the Navier-Stokes equations are shown to be well-posed in Sobolev spaces. In Section 5, we give a theorem on singularity formation: if positive solutions of these quasilinear equations ever touch down and obtain a value of zero, then the solutions must blow up in the space H4.H^{4}.

2. The linear problem

2.1. Main ideas and instructive examples

The following heuristics and special cases provide some crucial ideas for how we proceed. The first special case we consider is

(3) ut=a0​ux​x​x−b0​ux​xwithx∈[0,2​π]u_{t}=a_{0}u_{xxx}-b_{0}u_{xx}\quad{\textrm{with}}\quad x\in[0,2\pi]

where a0a_{0} and b0b_{0} are positive and constant and uu satisfies periodic boundary conditions. The equation can be solved via Fourier series:

u⁡(x,t)=∑k∈𝐙exp⁡(−i​a0​k3​t)​exp⁡(b0​k2​t)​ei​k​x​u^​(k,0).u(x,t)=\sum_{k\in{\bf Z}}\exp(-ia_{0}k^{3}t)\exp(b_{0}k^{2}t)e^{ikx}\widehat{u}(k,0).

Here u^​(k,0)\widehat{u}(k,0) are the coefficients of the Fourier series expansion of the initial data. A routine calculation shows that the right hand side of this equation, viewed as a map from 𝐑+×Hs{\bf{R}}^{+}\times H^{s} into HsH^{s} does not depend continuously on u⁡(x,0)u(x,0). This is due to the fact that exp⁡(b0​k2​t)\exp(b_{0}k^{2}t) grows extremely fast for large wave numbers kk. As such, (3) is ill-posed in precisely the same way that backwards heat equation is.

If bb is uniformly negative, this example illustrates that there is no chance for the dispersive effects to play a role (above, we had b⁡(x,t)=−b0<0b(x,t)=-b_{0}<0). However, if bb is localized and negative, there is reason to think that the dispersion can arrest blow up, as the following formal heuristic demonstrates. Specifically, consider the following:

(4) ut=a0​ux​x​x+b⁡(x)​ux​xwithx∈[−M,M]u_{t}=a_{0}u_{xxx}+b(x)u_{xx}\quad{\textrm{with}}\quad x\in[-M,M]

where

b⁡(x)={−b0<0, for x∈[0,L]0, otherwise.b(x)=\begin{cases}-b_{0}<0,&\text{ for $x\in[0,L]$}\\ 0,&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

Here 0<L≪M0<L\ll M. For simplicity, assume a0<0a_{0}<0. Consider a “wave packet” of amplitude μ0\mu_{0} and wave number k0k_{0} which is initially located to the left of x=0x=0. Such a wave packet will move with group speed associated to the equation ut=a0​ux​x​xu_{t}=a_{0}u_{xxx}, which is to say with speed

cg=3​|a0|​k02.c_{g}=3|a_{0}|k_{0}^{2}.

When the packet enters the interval [0,L][0,L], say at t=0t=0, it will be subjected to the effects of the backwards heat term, which will cause the amplitude to grow like

μ0​exp⁡(b0​k02​t),\mu_{0}\exp(b_{0}k_{0}^{2}t),

as was the case in (3). The wave packet will leave the interval [0,L][0,L] at time te​x​i​t=L/cgt_{exit}=L/c_{g} and thus the final amplitude of the packet is

(5) μ0​exp⁡(b0​k02​te​x​i​t)=μ0​exp⁡(b0​k02​L3​|a0|​k02)=μ0​exp⁡(L3​|b0a0|).\mu_{0}\exp\left(b_{0}k_{0}^{2}t_{exit}\right)=\mu_{0}\exp\left(b_{0}k_{0}^{2}{L\over 3|a_{0}|k_{0}^{2}}\right)=\mu_{0}\exp\left({L\over 3}\left|{b_{0}\over a_{0}}\right|\right).

See Figure 1. The growth of the amplitude during the wave packet’s passage through the destabilizing zone is independent of its wave number—the extremely rapid growth of high wave numbers is held in check by the fact that these highly oscillatory wave packets move very fast.

Therefore, if we presume that b⁡(x,t)b(x,t) is not everywhere negative, this heuristic indicates a plausible mechanism by which dispersion can arrest blowup. Note that equation (5) points to the importance of the ratio

δ⁡(x,t):=b⁡(x,t)|a⁡(x,t)|\delta(x,t):=\displaystyle{b(x,t)\over|a(x,t)|}

in determining the growth of the amplitude. We call δ⁡(x,t)\delta(x,t) the modified diffusion for the equation, for reasons which will become clear below.

We make this formal argument—which is closely related to the geometric optics heuristics described in [7]—precise in this article. Specifically, we give sufficient conditions on the coefficient functions a⁡(x,t),…a(x,t),\dots, e⁡(x,t)e(x,t) so that (2) is well-posed. In what follows Wk,p=Wk,p​(X)W^{k,p}=W^{k,p}(X) is the usual Sobolev space of periodic functions on XX, and Hn=Hn​(X)=Wn,2H^{n}=H^{n}(X)=W^{n,2}. Remark 2.

To demonstrate how surprising our results are, consider the following examples, all posed for x∈[0,2​π]x\in[0,2\pi]. Clearly, the initial value problem for the equation

ut=sin⁡(x)​ux​xu_{t}=\sin(x)u_{xx}

is ill-posed. However, if we add even a very small amount of dispersion, for instance,

ut=11023​ux​x​x+sin⁡(x)​ux​xu_{t}={1\over 10^{23}}u_{xxx}+\sin(x)u_{xx}

then the initial value problem for the equation is well-posed since the average modified diffusion in this case is equal to zero (since sin⁡(x)\sin(x) has average value zero).

Similarly, for any ε\varepsilon such that 0<ε<1,0<\varepsilon<1, the initial value problem for the equation

ut=(ε+sin⁡(x))​ux​xu_{t}=\left(\varepsilon+\sin(x)\right)u_{xx}

is again ill-posed. However, if we consider the equation with some dispersion, say

ut=11023​ux​x​x+(ε+sin⁡(x))​ux​x,u_{t}=\frac{1}{10^{23}}u_{xxx}+\left(\varepsilon+\sin(x)\right)u_{xx},

then since δ¯=1023​ε>0,\bar{\delta}=10^{23}\varepsilon>0, the initial value problem is well-posed. Morever, Theorem 2 states that even for a⁡(x,t)a(x,t) ludicrously small, as in this case, so long as ε>0\varepsilon>0, the equation is essentially parabolic even though, on a sizable fraction of the interval, there is a backwards heat operator acting.

Remark 3.

One can ask which of the assumptions are necessary as well as sufficient. We do not have definitive answers at this time, but some relevant information is known. The results in [2] and [7] strongly indicate that if a⁡(x,t)a(x,t) crosses zero for some xx with non-zero derivative, then (2) will be ill-posed. The regularity/integrability conditions in Assumption 1 can almost certainly be weakened, but doing so is likely technical and not terribly interesting at this time. A quick calculation shows that sending t→−tt\to-t in (2) results in an equation of the same form as (2) but reverses the sign of δ¯\bar{\delta}. The parabolic smoothing property in Theorem 2 indicates that it is highly unlikely that (2) would be well-posed backwards in time when δ¯​(t)>0\bar{\delta}(t)>0. These two facts together indicate that Assumption 3 is almost certainly necessary. We confirm this in the special case when the coefficients functions are time independent in Theorem 10 below.

Remark 4.

Assumption 2 allows us, without loss of generality, to take

a⁡(x,t)≥a0>0.a(x,t)\geq a_{0}>0.

And so, from this point on, a⁡(x,t)a(x,t) is presumed to be positive.

2.2. The change of variables and key estimate

Our goal is to find an a priori estimate for solutions u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) of (2) in the space HnH^{n}. It turns out that it this more easily done after changing dependent variables. Toward this end, we let gn​(x,t)g_{n}(x,t) be function which has the following three properties:

(7) u⁡(x,t):=gn​(x,t)​v​(x,t).u(x,t):=g_{n}(x,t)v(x,t).

Lemma 5.

Fix n∈𝐍n\in{\bf N} with n≥4n\geq 4. Suppose that A,B,C,D∈Wn,∞A,B,C,D\in W^{n,\infty}. Then there exists κ>0\kappa>0 (which depends only on nn, MM and the Wn,∞W^{n,\infty} norms of A,B,CA,B,C and DD) such that, for all ϕ∈Hn\phi\in H^{n}:

Now that we have selected gng_{n} we can prove that (8), and consequently (2), is well-posed. We will first prove uniqueness and continuous dependence of solutions, and we will then prove existence. This portion of the proof is similar to the proof that uniformly elliptic operators have eigenvalues which tend to infinity in [9]. Note that we are viewing LL as an unbounded linear operator from L2L^{2} to itself whose domain is H3H^{3}.

Since we are working on the periodic interval, LL is a relatively compact perturbation of ∂x3\partial_{x}^{3}. Thus we have σe​s​s(L)=σe​s​s(∂x3)={}\sigma_{ess}(L)=\sigma_{ess}(\partial_{x}^{3})=\left\{\right\}. This implies that the resolvent set of LL is nonempty. Let ω\omega be a point in the resolvent. Theorem 18.

Let w0∈Hnw_{0}\in H^{n} satisfy (58). Then, there exists T>0T>0 such that the initial value problem (56), (57) has a solution w∈C⁡([0,T],𝒪).w\in C([0,T];\mathcal{O}).

For ϵ∈(0,1),\epsilon\in(0,1), the functions wϵ{w^{\epsilon}} are all in the space C⁡([0,T],𝒪),C([0,T];\mathcal{O}), which implies that for all ϵ∈(0,1),\epsilon\in(0,1), for all t∈[0,T],t\in[0,T], we have the uniform bound ‖wϵ​(⋅,t)‖Hn≤2​‖w0‖Hn.\|{w^{\epsilon}}(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{n}}\leq 2\|w_{0}\|_{H^{n}}. |wϵ​(x,t)|≤C,|wxϵ​(x,t)|≤C,|wtϵ​(x,t)|≤C.|{w^{\epsilon}}(x,t)|\leq C,\qquad|{w^{\epsilon}_{x}}(x,t)|\leq C,\qquad|{w^{\epsilon}_{t}}(x,t)|\leq C.

Together with the uniform bound and an elementary interpolation inequality, this implies that the limit, w,w, is in C⁡([0,T],Hn′),C([0,T];H^{n^{\prime}}), for any 0≤n′<n.0\leq n^{\prime}<n.

Furthermore, pointwise in time, wϵ{w^{\epsilon}} is uniformly bounded in Hn,H^{n}, so there is a weak limit of a subsequence (since the unit ball of a Hilbert space is weakly compact) in Hn.H^{n}. By uniqueness of limits, this implies that for all t,t, we have w⁡(⋅,t)∈Hn.w(\cdot,t)\in H^{n}. We now want to show that w∈C⁡([0,T],Hn),w\in C([0,T];H^{n}), and that ww solves the non-mollified equation.

To show that ww solves the non-mollified evolution equation, we integrate the mollified evolution equation in time:

All that remains is to demonstrate the highest regularity. We will begin by showing that ‖w‖Hn\|w\|_{H^{n}} is continuous as a function of time. We start by showing that the norm is right-continuous at t=0.t=0. By Fatou’s Lemma, we have

‖w⁡(⋅,0)‖Hn2≤lim inft→0+‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖Hn2.\|w(\cdot,0)\|_{H^{n}}^{2}\leq\liminf_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}\|w(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{n}}^{2}.

Given t∗∈(0,T),t^{*}\in(0,T), we consider t∗t^{*} as a new initial time. We may solve the initial value problem starting from time t∗,t^{*}, with initial data w⁡(⋅,t∗).w(\cdot,t^{*}). By the previous argument, we see that this solution is right-continuous at time t=t∗.t=t^{*}. By the uniqueness theorem, we know that this solution starting from time t∗t^{*} and the previous solution, w,w, are the same. We sum up our results for the K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) equation in the following corollary:

Corollary 19.

Let nn be an integer such that n≥4.n\geq 4. Let XX be a periodic interval. Let a0>0.a_{0}>0. Let u0∈Hnu_{0}\in H^{n} be such that u0​(x)>a0u_{0}(x)>a_{0} for all x∈X.x\in X. Then there exists T>0T>0 and u∈C⁡([0,T],Hn)u\in C([0,T];H^{n}) such that for all x∈Xx\in X and for all t∈[0,T],t\in[0,T], uu satisfies u⁡(x,t)>a0/2,u(x,t)>a_{0}/2, and uu is the unique solution of the initial value problem (1) with u​(x,0)=u0​(x).u(x,0)=u_{0}(x).

Let n′n^{\prime} be given such that 0≤n′<n,0\leq n^{\prime}<n, and let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 be given. There exists δ>0\delta>0 such that for any v0∈Hnv_{0}\in H^{n} such that v0​(x)>a0v_{0}(x)>a_{0} for all x∈Xx\in X and such that ‖v0−u0‖Hn≤δ,\|v_{0}-u_{0}\|_{H^{n}}\leq\delta, the solution, v,v, of the initial value problem (1) with v​(x,0)=v0​(x)v(x,0)=v_{0}(x) satisfies v∈C⁡([0,T],Hn),v\in C([0,T];H^{n}), and

supt∈[0,T]‖u⁡(⋅,t)−v⁡(⋅,t)‖Hn′<ϵ.\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|u(\cdot,t)-v(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{n^{\prime}}}<\epsilon.

4. Other examples of quasilinear equations

In this section, we give additional examples of quasilinear equations for which our method gives a short-time well-posedness result. Like (1), these are also equations in which the dispersive effect appears nonlinearly. The first additional example is the Harry Dym equation, and the other examples arise in numerical analysis of finite difference schemes.

4.1. Well-posedness of the Harry Dym Equation

The Harry Dym equation is

(75) ut=u3​ux​x​x.u_{t}=u^{3}u_{xxx}.

This is a completely integrable equation [11] which has been shown to have applications in interfacial fluid dynamics [18]. We consider this with the initial condition

(76) u​(x,0)=u0​(x).u(x,0)=u_{0}(x).

As in the case of the K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) equation, we can show that the initial value problem for the Harry Dym equation is well-posed for H4H^{4} initial data which is bounded away from zero. The argument is completely analogous to the K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) case, so we only present the essential step, which is the HnH^{n} energy estimate. When providing all the details of the well-posedness proof, as we have done for the K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) equation, the energy estimate must in fact be carried out for a mollified version of the equation; in this section, we proceed informally, and present the energy estimate without first introducing mollifiers. Certainly, however, all of the details of the present argument can be carried out carefully as in the preceding section. We remark that, as in the case of the K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) equation, the average modified diffusion, δ¯,\bar{\delta}, that we defined before is identically zero; in the case of the Harry Dym equation, this is because there is no ux​xu_{xx} term present in (75).

Two conserved quantities for the Harry Dym equation are the following:

∫X1u⁡(x,t)​𝑑x,∫X1u2​(x,t)​𝑑x.\int_{X}\frac{1}{u(x,t)}\ dx,\qquad\int_{X}\frac{1}{u^{2}(x,t)}\ dx.

One view of the energy estimate which we are about to perform is that we are generalizing the first of these. We can take the view that the first of these conserved quantities tells us that the L2L^{2} norm of u−1/2u^{-1/2} is conserved by the evolution.

Let nn be an integer, such that n≥4.n\geq 4. We make the choice β=1n−12,\beta=\displaystyle\frac{1}{n-\frac{1}{2}}, following the same construction as used for (1) above. Note that, as before, this implies β∈(0,1);\beta\in(0,1); furthermore, we also have 3​β∈(0,1).3\beta\in(0,1). As before, we define w=u1β,w=u^{\frac{1}{\beta}}, so that u=wβ.u=w^{\beta}. From the previous section, we have the following relevant formulas:

ut=β​wβ−1​wt,u_{t}=\beta w^{\beta-1}w_{t},
ux​x​x=β⁡(β−1)​(β−2)​wβ−3​wx3+3​β​(β−1)​wβ−2​wx​wx​x+β​wβ−1​wx​x​x.u_{xxx}=\beta(\beta-1)(\beta-2)w^{\beta-3}w_{x}^{3}+3\beta(\beta-1)w^{\beta-2}w_{x}w_{xx}+\beta w^{\beta-1}w_{xxx}.

Combining these, we find the evolution equation for w:w:

(77) wt=w3​β​wx​x​x+3​(β−1)​w3​β−1​wx​wx​x+(β−1)​(β−2)​w3​β−2​wx3.w_{t}=w^{3\beta}w_{xxx}+3(\beta-1)w^{3\beta-1}w_{x}w_{xx}+(\beta-1)(\beta-2)w^{3\beta-2}w_{x}^{3}.

We apply the operator ∂xn\partial_{x}^{n} to (77):

(78) ∂xnwt=w3​β​∂xn+3w+(3​β+3​β​n−3)​w3​β−1​wx​∂xn+2w+F1​[w]​∂xn+1w+F2​[w],\partial_{x}^{n}w_{t}=w^{3\beta}\partial_{x}^{n+3}w+(3\beta+3\beta n-3)w^{3\beta-1}w_{x}\partial_{x}^{n+2}w+F_{1}[w]\partial_{x}^{n+1}w+F_{2}[w],

where

(79) F1​[w]=(n2)​∂x2(w3​β)+3​(β−1)​n​(w3​β−1​wx)x+3​(β−1)​w3​β−1​wx​x+3​(β−1)​(β−2)​w3​β−2​wx2,F_{1}[w]={n\choose 2}\partial_{x}^{2}(w^{3\beta})+3(\beta-1)n(w^{3\beta-1}w_{x})_{x}\\ +3(\beta-1)w^{3\beta-1}w_{xx}+3(\beta-1)(\beta-2)w^{3\beta-2}w_{x}^{2},

and

(80) F2​[w]=∑k=3n(nk)⁡(∂xkw3​β)​(∂xn−k+3w)+∑ℓ=1n(nℓ)⁡(∂xℓw3​β−1)​(∂xn−ℓ+1w)​wx​x+3(β−1)∑k=2n−1∑ℓ=1k(nk)(kℓ)(∂xℓw3​β−1)(∂xk−ℓ+1w)(∂xn−k+2w)+(∑k=1s−1(∂xk(3​w3​β−2​wx2))​(∂xn+1−kw))+∂xn−1((∂xw3​β−2)​wx3).F_{2}[w]=\sum_{k=3}^{n}{n\choose k}(\partial_{x}^{k}w^{3\beta})(\partial_{x}^{n-k+3}w)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}{n\choose\ell}(\partial_{x}^{\ell}w^{3\beta-1})(\partial_{x}^{n-\ell+1}w)w_{xx}\\ +3(\beta-1)\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}{n\choose k}{k\choose\ell}(\partial_{x}^{\ell}w^{3\beta-1})(\partial_{x}^{k-\ell+1}w)(\partial_{x}^{n-k+2}w)\\ +\left(\sum_{k=1}^{s-1}(\partial_{x}^{k}(3w^{3\beta-2}w_{x}^{2}))(\partial_{x}^{n+1-k}w)\right)+\partial_{x}^{n-1}((\partial_{x}w^{3\beta-2})w_{x}^{3}).

Since F1​[w]F_{1}[w] includes at most second derivatives of w,w, we can bound the L∞L^{\infty} norm of F1​[w]F_{1}[w] in terms of ‖w‖Hn.\|w\|_{H^{n}}. Since F2​[w]F_{2}[w] includes at most nn-many derivatives of w,w, we can bound the L2L^{2} norm of F2​[w]F_{2}[w] in terms of ‖w‖Hn.\|w\|_{H^{n}}.

We proceed to the energy estimate. We define the energy, E⁡(t),E(t), to be

E⁡(t)=12​∫Xw2+(∂xnw)2​𝑑x.E(t)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{X}w^{2}+(\partial_{x}^{n}w)^{2}\ dx.

Then, differentiating, we find the following:

d​Ed​t=∫Xw​wt+(∂xnw)​(∂xnwt)​𝑑x.\frac{dE}{dt}=\int_{X}ww_{t}+(\partial_{x}^{n}w)(\partial_{x}^{n}w_{t})\ dx.

Clearly, since n≥4,n\geq 4, we can bound ∫Xw​wt​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{X}ww_{t}\ dx in terms of E.E. Also, the contributions from F1F_{1} and F2F_{2} are bounded in terms of E.E.

The remaining piece that we must concern ourselves with is

∫X(∂xnw)​w3​β​∂xn+3w+(3​β+3​β​n−3)​(∂xnw)​w3​β−1​wx​∂xn+2w​𝑑x.\int_{X}(\partial_{x}^{n}w)w^{3\beta}\partial_{x}^{n+3}w+(3\beta+3\beta n-3)(\partial_{x}^{n}w)w^{3\beta-1}w_{x}\partial_{x}^{n+2}w\ dx.

We integrate the first term by parts:

∫X−(∂xn+1w)w3​β∂xn+2w+(3βn−3)(∂xnw)wx∂xn+2wdx.\int_{X}-(\partial_{x}^{n+1}w)w^{3\beta}\partial_{x}^{n+2}w+(3\beta n-3)(\partial_{x}^{n}w)w_{x}\partial_{x}^{n+2}w\ dx.

We recognize a perfect derivative in the first term, and we integrate both terms by parts:

∫X(3​β2−3​β​n+3)​w3​β−1​wx​(∂xn+1w)2−(3​β​n−3)​(∂xnw)​wx​x​∂xn+1w​𝑑x.\int_{X}\left(\frac{3\beta}{2}-3\beta n+3\right)w^{3\beta-1}w_{x}(\partial_{x}^{n+1}w)^{2}-(3\beta n-3)(\partial_{x}^{n}w)w_{xx}\partial_{x}^{n+1}w\ dx.

Since β=1n−12,\beta=\displaystyle\frac{1}{n-\frac{1}{2}}, the first of these terms is identically zero. Performing one more integration by parts, we see that the final term is bounded in terms of the energy.

Theorem 20.

Let nn be an integer such that n≥4.n\geq 4. Let XX be a periodic interval. Let a0>0.a_{0}>0. Let u0∈Hnu_{0}\in H^{n} be such that u0​(x)>a0u_{0}(x)>a_{0} for all x∈X.x\in X. Then there exists T>0T>0 and u∈C⁡([0,T],Hn)u\in C([0,T];H^{n}) such that for all x∈Xx\in X and for all t∈[0,T],t\in[0,T], uu satisfies u⁡(x,t)>a0/2,u(x,t)>a_{0}/2, and uu is the unique solution of the initial value problem (75), (76).

Let n′n^{\prime} be given such that 0≤n′<n,0\leq n^{\prime}<n, and let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 be given. There exists δ>0\delta>0 such that for any v0∈Hnv_{0}\in H^{n} such that v0​(x)>a0v_{0}(x)>a_{0} for all x∈Xx\in X and such that ‖v0−u0‖Hn≤δ,\|v_{0}-u_{0}\|_{H^{n}}\leq\delta, the solution, v,v, of the initial value problem (75) with v​(x,0)=v0​(x)v(x,0)=v_{0}(x) satisfies v∈C⁡([0,T],Hn),v\in C([0,T];H^{n}), and

supt∈[0,T]‖u⁡(⋅,t)−v⁡(⋅,t)‖Hn′<ϵ.\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|u(\cdot,t)-v(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{n^{\prime}}}<\epsilon.

4.2. Effective equations for finite difference schemes

In the paper [10], Goodman and Lax found that a certain finite difference scheme for the KdV equation has as an modified equation

(81) ut+u​ux+16​Δ2​u​ux​x​x=0,u_{t}+uu_{x}+\frac{1}{6}\Delta^{2}uu_{xxx}=0,

where Δ\Delta is the constant spatial step. Similarly, in studying a finite-difference scheme for a nonlocal dispersive equation, Zumbrun found the following modified equation [19]:

(82) ut+(u2)x=−c2​a2​(u​ux​x)x,u_{t}+(u^{2})_{x}=-c_{2}a^{2}(uu_{xx})_{x},

where c2c_{2} and aa are constants.

Slight variations of the arguments of the previous sections, which we will not repeat, imply that both of these are well-posed in H4,H^{4}, for initial data bounded away from zero. The important point is that as for the K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) equation and the Harry Dym equation, the average modified diffusion for (81) and for (82) is identically zero.

5. Remarks on singularity formation

We mention some further results related to singularity formation; these results hold for all of the quasilinear equations we have studied. These singularity formation results stem from theorems in [3] on positivity preservation for equations with the form

ut=u​F​[u]+ux​G​[x],u_{t}=uF[u]+u_{x}G[x],

where FF and GG are operators which can include uu and derivatives of u.u. (We note that the paper [8] also contains a positivity preservation theorem for the K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) equation.) The following theorem is a version of Theorem 6 of [3], which is proved using ideas from [5]:

Theorem 21.

Let T>0T>0 and let u∈C⁡([0,T],H4​(X))u\in C([0,T];H^{4}(X)) be a solution of (1), (75), (81), or (82). For each t∈[0,T],t\in[0,T], let m⁡(t)=infx∈Xu⁡(x,t).m(t)=\inf_{x\in X}u(x,t). Then, for all t∈[0,T],t\in[0,T], we have sgn⁡(m⁡(t))=sgn⁡(m⁡(0)).\mathrm{sgn}(m(t))=\mathrm{sgn}(m(0)).

The following corollary is an immediate consequence of this:

Corollary 22.

Let n∈𝐍n\in{\bf{N}} with n≥4.n\geq 4. Let a0>0.a_{0}>0. Let u0∈Hn​(X)u_{0}\in H^{n}(X) be such that u0​(x)>a0,u_{0}(x)>a_{0}, for all x∈X.x\in X. Let uu be the solution of the initial value problem for (1), (75), (81), or (82), with u​(x,0)=u0​(x).u(x,0)=u_{0}(x). Assume there exists x∗∈Xx_{*}\in X and t∗>0t_{*}>0 such that u⁡(x∗,t∗)=0.u(x_{*},t_{*})=0. Then there exists t∗⁣∗∈(0,t∗]t_{**}\in(0,t_{*}] such that

limt→t∗⁣∗−‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖4=+∞.\lim_{t\rightarrow t_{**}^{-}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{4}=+\infty.
